analysis.one_liner: Makes the oil industry's spill-cleanup tax permanent and funds oil spill prevention and response with it.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by two Republican senators, died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make permanent the excise tax that oil companies pay per barrel to fill the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund, the fund that pays to clean up oil spills and compensate victims, and it would broaden that tax to cover tar-sands-style bitumen for the first time. It would double how much the fund can spend on any single spill and on natural resource damage claims, let the Coast Guard draw up to $100 million quickly from the fund during a disaster, and use fund interest for annual grants to states for spill prevention and to universities for spill research, including in icy waters. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, coastal residents, fishing and tourism businesses, and taxpayers in oil-spill-prone states would have gained: a permanently solvent, industry-financed fund would cover more of each disaster ($2 billion per incident instead of $1 billion), and state prevention grants would fund equipment upgrades, training, and removal of derelict vessels before spills happen. Universities specializing in cold-water and ice-affected spill research would have gotten dedicated grant money, and the Coast Guard could have drawn up to $100 million immediately for a response instead of waiting on appropriations.

how_it_helps.text: Doubles what the industry-funded Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund can spend on any single spill (from $1 billion to $2 billion) and on natural resource damage claims (from $500 million to $1 billion), with the new caps indexed to inflation — meaning more of a major spill gets paid by the fund rather than by victims or the general treasury.

Creates two grant programs paid from the fund's interest: $25 million a year for states with oil terminals to upgrade spill equipment and training, address aging oil storage infrastructure, and remove derelict vessels, and $10 million every two years for universities doing oil spill response and prevention research, including in ice-impacted environments.

Lets the Coast Guard draw advances of up to $100 million from the fund so federal spill response isn't delayed waiting for Congress to appropriate money mid-disaster, with reports to Congress on every advance.

Makes the per-barrel oil tax that finances the fund permanent instead of letting it expire, and broadens it to cover bitumen and oil derived from bitumen (tar-sands crude), so more of the industry that creates spill risk pays into the cleanup fund.

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers and petroleum importers, who would have paid the spill tax permanently rather than only through a set end date, and who would have paid it on bitumen and tar-sands-derived oil for the first time. Like most excise taxes, that per-barrel cost would tend to be passed along in fuel and petroleum product prices. The doubled spending caps also draw the fund down faster, which is what triggers the tax's built-in suspension periods.

drawbacks.text: The tax is on crude oil and imported petroleum products, and excise costs like this are generally passed through to consumers in fuel prices, so drivers and shippers would bear part of the permanent per-barrel charge.

The bill automatically suspends the tax whenever the fund's unobligated balance exceeds $7 billion and restarts it only after the balance falls to $5 billion — so industry payments stop when the fund is full, while the bill simultaneously doubles how fast the fund can spend, which could leave it thinner between spills than either side intends.

The university research grants are written for a narrow set of institutions: eligibility requires oil-spill expertise, a location where future development would intensify spill threats, and for ice-related work, significant experience in ice-impacted environments — criteria that point strongly toward a small number of schools, in practice favoring Alaska-centric institutions rather than spill-prone regions generally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its merits this was a fairly conventional polluter-pays bill: a modest per-barrel charge on the industry that creates spill risk, financing a larger cleanup fund, faster federal response, and state prevention grants — a small, spread-out cost against real protection in the rare but catastrophic event. Its weakest points are the automatic tax holiday whenever the fund fills up and the narrow tailoring of the research grants toward cold-water institutions. But the bill never got far enough for those design questions to be litigated: it had only two Senate supporters and the Finance Committee took no action on it at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or moved it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dan Sullivan introduced the bill on March 25, 2019; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, whose jurisdiction covers the trust fund's financing tax.

That was the last action of any kind: the bill never received a hearing, a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and all bills not passed die when a Congress ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil producers and petroleum importers came out ahead — they avoided a permanently extended per-barrel tax and, for the first time, a tax on tar-sands bitumen. Coastal communities and taxpayers got no new spill protections or prevention funding.

for.name: Sen. Dan Sullivan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which ties the trust fund's financing tax permanently to spill response and writes grant eligibility around spill research in ice-impacted environments and state prevention programs.

for.name: One Senate Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Chuck Grassley)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split exists in the record; the bill's two supporters, sponsor Dan Sullivan and one cosponsor, were both Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would make the per-barrel trust fund tax permanent and apply it to bitumen and tar-sands-derived oil for the first time, while the fund it finances pays double for major spills. Its death means the industry kept a tax scheduled to lapse and a narrower tax base.

industries.industry: Universities with ocean, coastal, and Arctic spill research programs
industries.note: A dedicated $10 million biennial stream for spill response and prevention research, with criteria that strongly favor institutions experienced in ice-impacted environments, would have gone to these schools without annual appropriations.

industries.industry: State governments with marine oil terminals and facilities
industries.note: Annual $25 million grants would have funded prevention equipment, training facilities, risk assessments, and derelict vessel removal in states facing constant spill threats.

industries.industry: Bulk oil storage and marine transportation
industries.note: State grants would have targeted aging bulk oil storage and transportation infrastructure and the fund would cover more spill removal costs, but the industry's shippers would also bear the extended per-barrel tax on the petroleum moving through their facilities.
